According to the Chinese remainder theorem, which of the following systems of congruences has a unique solution modulo $60?$ 

$$
\text{I.}\,\{\begin{aligned}x≡1 & (\text{mod}\,3) \\ x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,4) \\ x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}\,\text{II.}\,\{\begin{aligned}x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}\,\text{III.}\,\{\begin{aligned}x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}\,
$$

The Chinese remainder theorem states that if the natural numbers ${n}_{1},{n}_{2},…,{n}_{k}$ are pairwise coprime, meaning that $\text{gcd}({n}_{i},{n}_{j})=1$ whenever $i\ne j,$ then for any integers ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},…,{a}_{k}$ the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x≡{a}_{1} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{1}) \\ x≡{a}_{2} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{2}) \\ \,⋮ \\ x≡{a}_{k} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{k})\end{aligned}
$$

has a unique solution modulo ${n}_{1}{n}_{2}⋯{n}_{k}.$

Let's now inspect each of the given systems in turn.

- The theorem applies to system I. The numbers $3,$ $4,$ and $5$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $3\cdot 4\cdot 5=60.$

- The theorem does *not* apply to system II since $6$ and $10$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(6,10)=2>1
$$

- The theorem applies to system III. The numbers $5$ and $12$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $5\cdot 12=60.$

So, the correct answer is "I and III only."

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =1+3t \\  & =1+3(2+4s) \\  & =7+12s.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Find the smallest natural number solution to the system of linear congruences below.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,3) \\ x≡4 & (\text{mod}\,7) \\ x≡5 & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $3,$ $7,$ and $8$ are coprime, then according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $3\cdot 7\cdot 8=168.$

We will solve the system in two steps.

**Step 1.** Find the common solution for the first and second congruences of the system.

From the first congruence, we get

$$
x≡2\,(\text{mod}\,3)\,⟹\,x=2+3t,\,t\in Z.
$$

Substituting this into the second congruence, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡4 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ 2+3t & ≡4 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ 3t & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $7$ is a relatively small modulus, we can solve it by trial and error. We have that $5\cdot 3≡1\,(\text{mod}\,7).$ So, we multiply both sides by $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3t & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ 5\cdot 3t & ≡10 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ t & ≡3 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $t=3+7s,$ where $s\in Z.$ Substituting this into the expression for $x,$ we get the common solution for the first and second congruences:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2+3t \\  & =2+3(3+7s) \\  & =11+21s\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Find the common solution of all three congruences.

Now, substituting the common solution of the first two congruences into the third congruence, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡5 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,8) \\ 11+21s & ≡5 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,8) \\ 21s & ≡-6 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,8) \\ 5s & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $8$ is a relatively small modulus, by trial and error, we have that $5\cdot 5≡1\,(\text{mod}\,8).$ So, we multiply both sides by $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5s & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,8) \\ 5\cdot 5s & ≡10 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,8) \\ s & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $s=2+8u,$ where $u\in Z.$ Substituting this into the expression for the common solution of the first two congruences, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =11+21s \\  & =11+21(2+8u) \\  & =53+168u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x≡53\,(\text{mod}\,168)$ is the unique solution modulo $168,$ and $x=53$ is the smallest natural number solution to the system.

\{\begin{aligned}x≡1 & (\text{mod}\,2) \\ x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,3) \\ x≡5 & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}

We will solve the system in two steps.

**Step 1.** Find the common solution for the first and second congruences of the system.

From the first congruence, we get

$$
x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,2)\,⟹\,x=1+2t,\,t\in Z.
$$

Substituting this into the second congruence, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3) \\ 1+2t & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3) \\ 2t & ≡1 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $3$ is a relatively small modulus, we can solve it by trial and error. We have that $2\cdot 2≡1\,(\text{mod}\,3).$ So, we multiply both sides by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2t & ≡1 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3) \\ 2\cdot 2t & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3) \\ t & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $t=2+3s,$ where $s\in Z.$ Substituting this into the expression for $x,$ we get the common solution for the first and second congruences:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =1+2t \\  & =1+2(2+3s) \\  & =5+6s\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Find the common solution of all three congruences.

Now, substituting the common solution of the first two congruences into the third congruence, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡5 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ 5+6s & ≡5 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ 6s & ≡0 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $7$ is a relatively small modulus, by trial and error, we have that $6\cdot 6≡1\,(\text{mod}\,7).$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}6s & ≡0 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ 6\cdot 6s & ≡0 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ s & ≡0 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $s=7u,$ where $u\in Z.$ Substituting this into the expression for the common solution of the first two congruences, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5+6s \\  & =5+6(7u) \\  & =5+42u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x≡5\,(\text{mod}\,42)$ is the unique solution modulo $42,$ and $x=5$ is the smallest natural number solution to the system.

canonical_examples.problem:
According to the Chinese remainder theorem, which of the following systems of congruences has a unique solution modulo $140?$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14274150/assets/b852381c8348d48780740adff5af410329d8078d19822e3a185b1847992fd92b.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Chinese remainder theorem states that if the natural numbers $n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k$ are pairwise coprime, meaning that $\text{gcd}(n_i,n_j)=1$ whenever $i \neq j,$ then for any integers $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k$ the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x≡{a}_{1} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{1}) \\ x≡{a}_{2} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{2}) \\ \,⋮ \\ x≡{a}_{k} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{k})\end{aligned}
$$

has a unique solution modulo $n_1 n_2 \cdots n_k.$

Let's now inspect each of the given systems in turn.

- The theorem applies to system I. The numbers $4,$ $5,$ and $7$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $4 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 = 140.$

- The theorem does *not* apply to system II since $10$ and $14$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(10,14)=2 > 1
$$

- The theorem applies to system III. The numbers $7$ and $20$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $7 \cdot 20 = 140.$

So, the correct answer is "I and III only."

                    Solving a System of Two Linear Congruences
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the smallest natural number solution to the system of linear congruences below.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x≡1 & (\text{mod}\,2) \\ x≡5 & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $2$ and $7$ are coprime, then according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $2 \cdot 7 = 14.$

From the first congruence, we get

$$
x \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:2)
\qquad
\Longrightarrow
\qquad 
x = 1 + 2t, \quad t \in \mathbb{Z}.
$$

Substituting this into the second congruence, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡5 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ 1+2t & ≡5 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ 2t & ≡4 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $7$ is a relatively small modulus, by trial and error, we have that $4 \cdot 2 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:7).$ So, we multiply both sides by $4\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2t & ≡4 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ 4\cdot 2t & ≡16 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7) \\ t & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $t = 2 + 7s,$ where $s \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =1+2t \\  & =1+2(2+7s) \\  & =5+14s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x \equiv 5 \: (\text{mod}\:14)$ is the unique solution modulo $14,$ and $x=5$ is the smallest natural number solution to the system.

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the smallest natural number solution to the system of linear congruences below.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x≡1 & (\text{mod}\,2) \\ x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,3) \\ x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $2,$ $3,$ and $5$ are coprime, then according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 = 30.$

We will solve the system in two steps.

**Step 1.** Find the common solution for the first and second congruences of the system.

From the first congruence, we get

$$
x \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:2)
\qquad
\Longrightarrow
\qquad 
x = 1 + 2t, \quad t \in \mathbb{Z}.
$$

Substituting this into the second congruence, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3) \\ 1+2t & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3) \\ 2t & ≡1 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $3$ is a relatively small modulus, we can solve it by trial and error. We have that $2 \cdot 2 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:3).$ So, we multiply both sides by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2t & ≡1 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3) \\ 2\cdot 2t & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3) \\ t & ≡2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,3)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $t = 2 + 3s,$ where $s \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for $x,$ we get the common solution for the first and second congruences:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =1+2t \\  & =1+2(2+3s) \\  & =5+6s\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Find the common solution of all three congruences.

Now, substituting the common solution of the first two congruences into the third congruence, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡3 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ 5+6s & ≡3 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ 6s & ≡-2 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ s & ≡3 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $s = 3 + 5u,$ where $u \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for the common solution of the first two congruences, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5+6s \\  & =5+6(3+5u) \\  & =23+30u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x \equiv 23 \: (\text{mod}\:30)$ is the unique solution modulo $30,$ and $x=23$ is the smallest natural number solution to the system.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The Chinese remainder theorem states that if the natural numbers $n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k$ are pairwise coprime, meaning that $\text{gcd}(n_i,n_j)=1$ whenever $i \neq j,$ then for any integers $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k$ the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x≡{a}_{1} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{1}) \\ x≡{a}_{2} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{2}) \\ \,⋮ \\ x≡{a}_{k} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{k})\end{aligned}
$$

has a unique solution modulo $n_1 n_2 \cdots n_k.$

For example, suppose that we want to find the smallest natural number solution to the following system of linear congruences:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x≡4 & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x≡7 & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

This system can be interpreted as follows. Suppose we have $x$ identical "bricks" and we know that:

- if we stack them in piles with $5$ bricks each, then the last remaining pile will contain $4$ bricks.

- if we stack them in piles with $9$ bricks each, then the last remaining pile will contain $7$ bricks.

How can we find the smallest possible number $x?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14274150/assets/dd89c8b56cd455b7aafa41cd8d305a7455246141851c49d26ba5cf955f87de7a.png)

First, we note that $5$ and $9$ are coprime. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $5 \cdot 9 = 45.$

From the first congruence, we get

$$
x \equiv 4 \: (\text{mod}\:5)
\qquad
\Longrightarrow
\qquad 
x = 4 + 5t, \quad t \in \mathbb{Z}.
$$

Substituting this into the second congruence, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡7 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,9) \\ 4+5t & ≡7 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,9) \\ 5t & ≡3 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $9$ is a relatively small modulus, we can find the multiplicative inverse of $5$ by trial and error. We find that $2 \cdot 5 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:9).$ So, we multiply both sides of the above congruence by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5t & ≡3 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,9) \\ 2\cdot 5t & ≡2\cdot 3 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,9) \\ t & ≡6 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $t = 6 + 9s,$ where $s \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting this into the expression for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4+5t \\  & =4+5(6+9s) \\  & =34+45s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x \equiv 34 \: (\text{mod}\:45)$ is the unique solution modulo $45.$ The solution $x=34$ is the smallest natural number solution to the system, and all other solutions are obtained by adding or subtracting multiples of $45$ to this solution. 

Finally, let's check that this is indeed correct. Substituting $x=34$ into the first congruence, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}34 & ≡4 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ 34-6(5) & ≡4 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ 4 & ≡4 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,5),\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting $x=34$ into the second congruence, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}34 & ≡7 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,9) \\ 34-3(9) & ≡7 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,9) \\ 7 & ≡7 &  & \,(\text{mod}\,9).\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
